claim: Approximately 500 lncRNAs were shown to be highly restricted in primary human endothelial cells (ECs).
source: In an effort to identify human endothelial cell (EC)-enriched lncRNAs,~500 lncRNAs were shown to be highly restricted in primary human ECs.
evidence: The abstract states that microarray profiling identified ~500 EC-restricted lncRNAs, which is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is located in the opposite strand of the EGFL7/miR-126 gene.
source: Among them, lncEGFL7OS, located in the opposite strand of the EGFL7/miR-126 gene, is regulated by ETS factors through a bidirectional promoter in ECs.
evidence: The genomic organization is described in the abstract and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is regulated by ETS factors through a bidirectional promoter in ECs.
source: Among them, lncEGFL7OS, located in the opposite strand of the EGFL7/miR-126 gene, is regulated by ETS factors through a bidirectional promoter in ECs.
evidence: The manuscript presents luciferase assays and siRNA experiments demonstrating ETS factor regulation of lncEGFL7OS.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is enriched in highly vascularized human tissues.
source: It is enriched in highly vascularized human tissues, and upregulated in the hearts of dilated cardiomyopathy patients.
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 2B shows lncEGFL7OS expression across different human tissues.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is upregulated in the hearts of dilated cardiomyopathy patients.
source: It is enriched in highly vascularized human tissues, and upregulated in the hearts of dilated cardiomyopathy patients.
evidence: Figure 2E shows qRT-PCR data comparing lncEGFL7OS expression in control and DCM patient hearts.

claim: LncEGFL7OS silencing impairs angiogenesis as shown by EC/fibroblast co-culture assays.
source: LncEGFL7OS silencing impairs angiogenesis as shown by EC/fibroblast co-culture, in vitro/in vivo and ex vivo human choroid sprouting angiogenesis assays, while lncEGFL7OS overexpression has the opposite function.
evidence: Figure 3A-B shows decreased capillary tube formation after lncEGFL7OS silencing in EC-fibroblast co-culture assays.

claim: LncEGFL7OS silencing impairs angiogenesis in in vivo Matrigel implantation assays.
source: LncEGFL7OS silencing impairs angiogenesis as shown by EC/fibroblast co-culture, in vitro/in vivo and ex vivo human choroid sprouting angiogenesis assays, while lncEGFL7OS overexpression has the opposite function.
evidence: Figure 3C-D demonstrates defective EC networking in vivo after lncEGFL7OS silencing.

claim: LncEGFL7OS silencing impairs ex vivo human choroid sprouting angiogenesis.
source: LncEGFL7OS silencing impairs angiogenesis as shown by EC/fibroblast co-culture, in vitro/in vivo and ex vivo human choroid sprouting angiogenesis assays, while lncEGFL7OS overexpression has the opposite function.
evidence: Figure 3F-H shows inhibition of human choroid sprouting after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: lncEGFL7OS overexpression enhances angiogenesis.
source: LncEGFL7OS silencing impairs angiogenesis as shown by EC/fibroblast co-culture, in vitro/in vivo and ex vivo human choroid sprouting angiogenesis assays, while lncEGFL7OS overexpression has the opposite function.
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C shows enhanced angiogenesis after lncEGFL7OS overexpression in EC-fibroblast co-culture assays.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is required for MAPK pathway activation by regulating EGFL7/miR-126 expression.
source: Mechanistically, lncEGFL7OS is required for MAPK and AKT pathway activation by regulating EGFL7/miR-126 expression.
evidence: Figure 5C shows reduced ERK1/2 phosphorylation after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is required for AKT pathway activation by regulating EGFL7/miR-126 expression.
source: Mechanistically, lncEGFL7OS is required for MAPK and AKT pathway activation by regulating EGFL7/miR-126 expression.
evidence: Figure 5C shows reduced AKT phosphorylation after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: MAX protein was identified as a lncEGFL7OS-interacting protein.
source: MAX protein was identified as a lncEGFL7OS-interacting protein that functions to regulate histone acetylation in the EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer.
evidence: Figure 6B shows RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) assays demonstrating MAX binding to lncEGFL7OS.

claim: MAX functions to regulate histone acetylation in the EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer.
source: MAX protein was identified as a lncEGFL7OS-interacting protein that functions to regulate histone acetylation in the EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer.
evidence: Figure 6F shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating that lncEGFL7OS overexpression increases H3K27 acetylation at the EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer region.

claim: CRISPR-mediated targeting of EGLF7/miR-126/lncEGFL7OS locus inhibits angiogenesis.
source: CRISPR-mediated targeting of EGLF7/miR-126/lncEGFL7OS locus inhibits angiogenesis, inciting therapeutic potential of targeting this locus.
evidence: Figure 8B-C shows that dCas9-KRAB-mediated targeting of the locus significantly represses angiogenesis in EC-fibroblast co-culture assays.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is a human/primate-specific EC-restricted lncRNA.
source: Our study establishes lncEGFL7OS as a human/primate-specific EC-restricted lncRNA critical for human angiogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript states that conserved homologous sequence of lncEGFL7OS only exists in humans and primates Rhesus monkey, but not in other lower vertebrate species including mice.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is critical for human angiogenesis.
source: Our study establishes lncEGFL7OS as a human/primate-specific EC-restricted lncRNA critical for human angiogenesis.
evidence: Multiple angiogenesis assays (EC-fibroblast co-culture, in vivo Matrigel, ex vivo human choroid sprouting) demonstrate the requirement of lncEGFL7OS for angiogenesis.

claim: Angiogenesis plays a critical role in tissue development and homeostasis.
source: Angiogenesis plays a critical role in tissue development and homeostasis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of vascular biology.

claim: Aberrant angiogenesis has been associated with numerous diseases, including heart disease, tumor growth, metastasis and age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
source: Aberrant angiogenesis has been associated with numerous diseases, including heart disease, tumor growth, metastasis and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Carmeliet, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carmeliet, 2003.

claim: Defective vascularization has been observed in human dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) patients.
source: Defective vascularization, usually associated with compensatory angiogenesis and vasculogenesis, has been observed in human dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) patients (Roura et al., 2007; Gavin et al., 1998; De Boer et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Roura et al., 2007; Gavin et al., 1998; De Boer et al., 2003.

claim: Methods to augment angiogenesis have been tested clinically for DCM.
source: Methods to augment angiogenesis have been tested clinically for DCM (Ylä-Herttuala et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ylä-Herttuala et al., 2017.

claim: Anti-angiogenic therapy, such as antibodies to vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF), has shown efficacy clinically in treating wet AMD.
source: Anti-angiogenic therapy, such as antibodies to vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF), has shown efficacy clinically in treating wet AMD, the leading blinding disease in the elderly (Brown et al., 2006; Rosenfeld et al., 2006; Zampros et al., 2012; Hurwitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2006; Rosenfeld et al., 2006; Zampros et al., 2012; Hurwitz et al., 2004.

claim: Wet AMD is the leading blinding disease in the elderly.
source: Anti-angiogenic therapy, such as antibodies to vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF), has shown efficacy clinically in treating wet AMD, the leading blinding disease in the elderly (Brown et al., 2006; Rosenfeld et al., 2006; Zampros et al., 2012; Hurwitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in ophthalmology.

claim: Some patients failed to respond to anti-VEGF treatment.
source: However, some patients failed to respond to anti-VEGF treatment.
evidence: This is a known clinical observation in the treatment of wet AMD.

claim: Anti-angiogenic therapies have shown efficacy in certain cancers when used alone or combined with chemotherapy.
source: Similarly, anti-angiogenic therapies have shown efficacy in certain cancers when used alone or combined with chemotherapy (Miller et al., 2007; Sandler et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2007; Sandler et al., 2006.

claim: Anti-angiogenic therapy has met several hurdles on its way to be a main option for cancer therapy, mainly due to drug resistance.
source: However, anti-angiogenic therapy has met several hurdles on its way to be an main option for cancer therapy, mainly due to drug resistance (Shojaei and Ferrara, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shojaei and Ferrara, 2007.

claim: Up to 90% of the human genome is transcribed.
source: It is now established that up to 90% of the human genome is transcribed, and the majority of these transcripts are non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) that do not encode proteins (Kapranov et al., 2007; Gerstein, 2012; Ecker, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kapranov et al., 2007; Gerstein, 2012; Ecker, 2012.

claim: The majority of transcripts from the human genome are non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) that do not encode proteins.
source: It is now established that up to 90% of the human genome is transcribed, and the majority of these transcripts are non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) that do not encode proteins (Kapranov et al., 2007; Gerstein, 2012; Ecker, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kapranov et al., 2007; Gerstein, 2012; Ecker, 2012.

claim: miRNAs include a group of small noncoding RNAs sized ~22 nucleotides that play important regulatory functions in numerous physiological and pathological processes, including angiogenesis.
source: miRNAs include a group of small noncoding RNAs sized ~22 nucleotides that play important regulatory functions in numerous physiological and pathological processes, including angiogenesis (Wang and Olson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang and Olson, 2009.

claim: LncRNAs represent a large group of long (typically >200 nt) noncoding RNAs, whose function is still largely enigmatic.
source: LncRNAs represent a large group of long (typically >200 nt) noncoding RNAs, whose function is still largely enigmatic (Ulitsky and Bartel, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ulitsky and Bartel, 2013.

claim: The study of lncRNAs in vascular biology is still in its infancy.
source: The study of lncRNAs in vascular biology is still in its infancy (Yu and Wang, 2018; MM and Goyal, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yu and Wang, 2018; MM and Goyal, 2016.

claim: Several lncRNAs, including MALAT1, MANTIS, PUNISHER, MEG3, MIAT, SENCR, GATA6-AS and STEEL, have been shown to regulate angiogenesis.
source: Several lncRNAs, including MALAT1 (Liu et al., 2014; Michalik et al., 2014), MANTIS (Leisegang et al., 2017), PUNISHER (Kurian et al., 2015), MEG3 (He et al., 2017; Qiu et al., 2016), MIAT (Yan et al., 2015), SENCR (Boulberdaa et al., 2016), GATA6-AS (Neumann et al., 2018) and STEEL (Man et al., 2018), have been shown to regulate angiogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: A microarray was performed to profile ~30,000 lncRNAs and ~26,000 coding transcripts using an Arraystar human LncRNA microarray v3.0 system.
source: To identify lncRNAs specific in ECs, a microarray was performed to profile ~30,000 lncRNAs and ~26,000 coding transcripts using an Arraystar human LncRNA microarray v3.0 system (Arraystar, Rockville, MD).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Three primary human EC lines and two non-EC lines at low passages were used in the microarray.
source: Three primary human EC lines and two non-EC lines at low passages, namely, human umbilical vein EC (HUVEC), human retinal EC (HREC), human choroidal EC (HCEC), human dermal fibroblast cell (HDF) and human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell lines, were used in the array.
evidence: This describes the cell lines used in the microarray experiment.

claim: Hierarchical cluster analysis of the array results validated the clustering of EC lines, which clearly separates from the HDF and RPE cell lines based on lncRNA and mRNA expression.
source: Hierarchical cluster analysis of the array results validated the clustering of EC lines, which clearly separates from the HDF and RPE cell lines based on lncRNA and mRNA expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: Figure 1A shows the hierarchical clustering analysis of the microarray data.

claim: lncRNAs appeared to be a stronger classifier to distinguish between EC and non-ECs than mRNAs.
source: Moreover, lncRNAs appeared to be a stronger classifier to distinguish between EC and non-ECs than mRNAs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 498 lncRNAs are enriched in all three EC lines for more than two folds compared to the non-ECs.
source: 498 lncRNAs are enriched in all three EC lines for more than two folds compared to the non-ECs (see Figure 1B for top 50 hits, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Figure 1B shows a heatmap of the top 50 enriched lncRNAs, and Supplementary file 1 contains the full list.

claim: Among the 498 EC-enriched lncRNAs, 308 are intergenic lncRNAs, 62 are sense overlapping lncRNAs, 83 are antisense lncRNAs, 23 are bidirectional lncRNAs, and 22 lncRNAs were previously identified as pseudogenes.
source: Among them, 308 are intergenic lncRNAs, 62 are sense overlapping lncRNAs, 83 are antisense lncRNAs, 23 are bidirectional lncRNAs, and 22 lncRNAs were previously identified as pseudogenes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Figure 1C shows a pie chart of the different classes of EC-enriched lncRNAs.

claim: 19 of the EC-enriched lncRNAs are known enhancer-like lncRNAs with nearby coding genes within 300 kb.
source: When these lncRNAs were cross-referenced with the enhancer-like lncRNAs, 19 of them are known enhancer-like lncRNAs with nearby coding genes within 300 kb (Supplementary file 2) (Ørom et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on cross-referencing with published data from Ørom et al., 2010.

claim: 91 lncRNAs have protein-coding genes within 10 kb of the lncRNA gene.
source: 91 lncRNAs have protein-coding genes within 10 kb of the lncRNA gene (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics analysis of the genomic locations of the EC-enriched lncRNAs.

claim: 27 of the 91 lncRNAs exhibited parallel expression pattern to the neighboring mRNAs in all 5 cell lines tested.
source: Moreover, 27 of the 91 lncRNAs exhibited parallel expression pattern to the neighboring mRNAs in all 5 cell lines tested, while three of them showed inverse expression pattern relationship with the neighboring mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the microarray expression data.

claim: Three of the 91 lncRNAs showed inverse expression pattern relationship with the neighboring mRNAs.
source: Moreover, 27 of the 91 lncRNAs exhibited parallel expression pattern to the neighboring mRNAs in all 5 cell lines tested, while three of them showed inverse expression pattern relationship with the neighboring mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the microarray expression data.

claim: Functional enrichment analysis shows that genes involved in heart development, chordate embryonic development, embryonic development ending in birth, blood vessel development, vasculature development, and metallopeptidase activity are highly represented in the associated lncRNAs with a false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 10%.
source: The following biological processes and genes are highly represented in the associated lncRNAs with a false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 10% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A): (1) heart development (NRP1, ECE1, FOXC2, PKD1, ZFPM2, FKBP1A, FOXP4); (2) chordate embryonic development (GATA2, SATB2, ECE1, LMX1B, FOXC2, PKD1, ZFPM2); (3) embryonic development ending in birth (GATA2, SATB2, ECE1, LMX1B, FOXC2, PKD1, ZFPM2); (4) blood vessel development (NRP1, EGFL7, ROBO4, FOXC2, PKD1, ZFPM2); (5) vasculature development (NRP1, EGFL7, ROBO4, FOXC2, PKD1, ZFPM2); and (6) metallopeptidase activity (ECE1, ADAMTS16, LTA4H, MMP25, ADAM15).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2A shows the functional enrichment analysis results.

claim: The existence of lncEGFL7OS was confirmed by RT-PCR cloning using human placental RACE-ready cDNAs and subsequent sequencing.
source: The existence of lncEGFL7OS was confirmed by RT-PCR cloning using human placental RACE-ready cDNAs and subsequent sequencing, and the size of lncEGFL7OS is consistent with deposited gene AF161442 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows the RACE-PCR product of lncEGFL7OS.

claim: The size of lncEGFL7OS is consistent with deposited gene AF161442.
source: The existence of lncEGFL7OS was confirmed by RT-PCR cloning using human placental RACE-ready cDNAs and subsequent sequencing, and the size of lncEGFL7OS is consistent with deposited gene AF161442 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the cloned sequence with the deposited gene sequence.

claim: Conserved homologous sequence of lncEGFL7OS only exists in humans and primates Rhesus monkey, but not in other lower vertebrate species including mice.
source: Interestingly, conserved homologous sequence of lncEGFL7OS only exists in humans and primates Rhesus monkey, but not in other lower vertebrate species including mice, suggesting lncEGFL7OS is an evolutionarily new gene in mammals.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics analysis of sequence conservation across species.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is an evolutionarily new gene in mammals.
source: Interestingly, conserved homologous sequence of lncEGFL7OS only exists in humans and primates Rhesus monkey, but not in other lower vertebrate species including mice, suggesting lncEGFL7OS is an evolutionarily new gene in mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that lncEGFL7OS is only conserved in humans and primates.

claim: LncEGFL7OS was found to be highly enriched in the human lung, placenta and heart.
source: LncEGFL7OS was found to be highly enriched in the human lung, placenta and heart, which are highly vascularized tissues (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows qRT-PCR data of lncEGFL7OS expression in different human tissues.

claim: Human EGFL7 has four isoforms, named as EGFL7A-D, but only EGFL7B and EGFL7C are detectable by RT-PCR in human tissues.
source: Human EGFL7 has four isoforms, named as EGFL7A-D, but only EGFL7B and EGFL7C are detectable by RT-PCR in human tissues.
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR experiments performed in the study.

claim: Both EGFL7B and EGFL7C are enriched in heart, kidney, bone marrow, uterus, thymus, thyroid, small intestine and placenta.
source: By qRT-PCR, both EGFL7B and EGFL7C are enriched in heart, kidney, bone marrow, uterus, thymus, thyroid, small intestine and placenta.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows qRT-PCR data of EGFL7B and EGFL7C expression in different human tissues.

claim: EGFL7B is more enriched in prostate.
source: Besides that, EGFL7B is more enriched in prostate, while EGFL7C is more enriched in lung and brain, suggesting a differential expression pattern of EGFL7 isoforms in humans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows qRT-PCR data of EGFL7B and EGFL7C expression in different human tissues.

claim: EGFL7C is more enriched in lung and brain.
source: Besides that, EGFL7B is more enriched in prostate, while EGFL7C is more enriched in lung and brain, suggesting a differential expression pattern of EGFL7 isoforms in humans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows qRT-PCR data of EGFL7B and EGFL7C expression in different human tissues.

claim: miR-126 is highly enriched in the bone marrow, lung and heart.
source: miR-126 is highly enriched in the bone marrow, lung and heart (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1C shows qRT-PCR data of miR-126 expression in different human tissues.

claim: lncEGFL7OS is expressed in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, but more in the nucleus of HUVECs.
source: By RT-PCR, lncEGFL7OS was shown to be expressed in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, but more in the nucleus of HUVECs (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows semi-quantitative RT-PCR data of lncEGFL7OS expression in nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions.

claim: The average copy number of lncEGFL7OS RNA in HUVECs is ~19.
source: By quantification, the average copy number of lncEGFL7OS RNA in HUVECs is ~19, which is in agreement with the copy number (23–28 copies) by qRT-PCR using in vitro transcribed lncEGFL7OS as control for copy number calculation (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on quantification of RNA FISH signals and qRT-PCR data.

claim: In the DCM hearts, the expression of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), a prominent marker for heart failure, was drastically upregulated.
source: In the DCM hearts, the expression of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), a prominent marker for heart failure, was drastically upregulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1D shows qRT-PCR data of ANP expression in control and DCM hearts.

claim: The expression of EC/EPC marker PECAM-1 was marginally increased in DCM hearts.
source: In line with the increased angiogenic factors, the expression of EC/EPC marker PECAM-1 was also marginally increased.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1D shows qRT-PCR data of PECAM-1 expression in control and DCM hearts.

claim: The expression of EGFL7B and EGFL7C was significantly upregulated in the hearts of DCM patients.
source: Interestingly, the expression of EGFL7B and EGFL7C, as well as pri-miR-126, was also significantly upregulated in the hearts of DCM patients.
evidence: Figure 2E shows qRT-PCR data of EGFL7B and EGFL7C expression in control and DCM hearts.

claim: The expression of pri-miR-126 was significantly upregulated in the hearts of DCM patients.
source: Interestingly, the expression of EGFL7B and EGFL7C, as well as pri-miR-126, was also significantly upregulated in the hearts of DCM patients.
evidence: Figure 2E shows qRT-PCR data of pri-miR-126 expression in control and DCM hearts.

claim: A critical regulatory element is located on EGFL7B promoter between lncEGFL7OS and EGFL7/miR-126.
source: A critical regulatory element is located on EGFL7B promoter between lncEGFL7OS and EGFL7/miR-126.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics analysis of the locus using ENCODE data.

claim: LncEGFL7OS DNA contains a region positive for epigenetic marks including histone H3 trimethylated lysine four methylation (H3K4Me1) and H3K27Ac, H3K4Me3, and binding sites for transcription factors MAX, MYC and RNA Polymerase (PolR) II.
source: Bioinformatics data from ENCODE indicate that LncEGFL7OS DNA contains a region positive for epigenetic marks including histone H3 trimethylated lysine four methylation (H3K4Me1) and H3K27Ac (mark poised and active enhancers), H3K4Me3 (marks promoter of protein coding genes), and binding sites for transcription factors MAX, MYC and RNA Polymerase (PolR) II.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics analysis of ENCODE data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ChIP PCR assay using antibodies against MAX/MYC, RNA Pol II and histone H3 trimethylated lysine 4 (H3K4me3) demonstrated the binding of these factors specifically to the region.
source: Consistently, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) PCR assay using antibodies against MAX/MYC, RNA Pol II and histone H3 trimethylated lysine 4 (H3K4me3) demonstrated the binding of these factors specifically to the region but not a non-relevant nearby region, indicating that this region is transcriptionally active (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating binding of these factors to the region.

claim: CpG islands were found in the region between lncEGFL7OS and EGFL7 transcripts.
source: Additional potential promoters were not found in the region between lncEGFL7OS and EGFL7 transcripts by bioinformatics approach. Instead, CpG islands were found in the region.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics analysis of the genomic sequence.

claim: CpG islands in mammalian promoter regions tend to show bidirectional promoter activity.
source: CpG islands in mammalian promoter regions tend to show bidirectional promoter activity (Antequera, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Antequera, 2003.

claim: Bidirectional promoters have been proposed to drive head-to-head gene transcription involving ncRNAs.
source: Bidirectional promoters have been proposed to drive head-to-head gene transcription involving ncRNAs (Uesaka et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uesaka et al., 2014.

claim: The putative lncEGFL7OS promoter in either sense or anti-sense direction exhibited similar activity under baseline in 293 T cells.
source: By luciferase assay, the promoter in either direction exhibited similar activity under baseline in 293 T cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: Figure 2G shows luciferase assay data testing the bidirectional promoter activity.

claim: ETS1 transcription factor significantly activated the promoter activity in either direction.
source: Moreover, ETS1 transcription factor significantly activated the promoter activity in either direction, while the ETS1mut that lacks the DNA-binding domain showed significantly reduced activation of the promoter (Wang et al., 2008a).
evidence: Figure 2G shows luciferase assay data demonstrating ETS1 activation of the promoter.

claim: ETS1mut that lacks the DNA-binding domain showed significantly reduced activation of the promoter.
source: Moreover, ETS1 transcription factor significantly activated the promoter activity in either direction, while the ETS1mut that lacks the DNA-binding domain showed significantly reduced activation of the promoter (Wang et al., 2008a).
evidence: Figure 2G shows luciferase assay data demonstrating reduced activation by ETS1mut.

claim: ETS factors have been shown to regulate miR-126 expression in ECs.
source: ETS factors have been shown to regulate miR-126 expression in ECs (Harris et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2010.

claim: Both lncEGFL7OS and pri-miR-126 were significantly reduced by ETS1/2 silencing.
source: Both genes were significantly reduced by ETS1/2 silencing, suggesting ETS factors control the expression of both lncEGFL7OS and EGFL7/miR-126 (Figure 2H).
evidence: Figure 2H shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating downregulation of lncEGFL7OS and pri-miR-126 after ETS1/2 silencing.

claim: si-lincEGFL7#1 or si-lncEGFL7OS#2 significantly repressed the formation of vascular tubules at 7 days after co-culture.
source: Compared to the control siRNA, si-lincEGFL7#1 or si-lncEGFL7OS#2 significantly repressed the formation of vascular tubules at 7 days after co-culture as shown by PECAM-1 staining and the subsequent quantification of the vascular tube length (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Figure 3A-B shows decreased capillary tube formation after lncEGFL7OS silencing in EC-fibroblast co-culture assays.

claim: Fewer networking was observed in the lncEGFL7OS-silenced EC group compared to the well-connected vessel structure in the controls in the in vivo Matrigel assay.
source: Compared to the well-connected vessel structure in the controls, fewer networking was observed in the lncEGFL7OS-silenced EC group (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Figure 3C-D shows defective EC networking in vivo after lncEGFL7OS silencing.

claim: Red blood cells and smooth muscle cells recruiting was detected in the formed vessels in the Matrigel assay.
source: Red blood cells and smooth muscle cells recruiting was detected in the formed vessels as proved by co-staining of human PECAM-1 and mouse Ter-119 (red blood cell marker) or mouse α-SMA (smooth muscle marker) staining, which suggests functionality of the vessels (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B show co-staining of PECAM-1 with Ter-119 and α-SMA.

claim: lncEGFL7OS siRNAs drastically repressed human choroid sprouting.
source: Compared to the control, lncEGFL7OS siRNAs drastically repressed human choroid sprouting, establishing a critical role for lncEGFL7OS in angiogenesis in human tissues (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: Figure 3F-G shows inhibition of human choroid sprouting after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: The EC identity of the sprouting cells was confirmed by ICAM-2 and isolectin B4 co-staining.
source: The EC identity of the sprouting cells was confirmed by ICAM-2 and isolectin B4 co-staining (Figure 3H).
evidence: Figure 3H shows ICAM-2 and isolectin B4 staining of the choroid sprouts.

claim: si-lncEGFL7OS#2 significantly decreased EC proliferation as shown by BrdU incorporation compared to the random control under starvation condition.
source: Under starvation condition, si-lincEGFL7#2 significantly decreased EC proliferation as shown by BrdU incorporation compared to the random control, while the effect from si-lncEGFL7OS#1 was not statistically significant (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows BrdU incorporation data after lncEGFL7OS silencing.

claim: The EC proliferation induced by VEGF treatment was significantly repressed by either si-lncEGFL7OS#1 or si-lncEGFL7OS#2.
source: However, the EC proliferation induced by VEGF treatment was significantly repressed by either si-lncEGFL7OS#1 or si-lncEGFL7OS#2.
evidence: Figure 4A shows BrdU incorporation data after lncEGFL7OS silencing with VEGF treatment.

claim: A significant increase in the percentage of cells in the G0/G1 phase was observed upon lncEGFL7OS knockdown.
source: A significant increase in the percentage of cells in the G0/G1 phase was observed upon lncEGFL7OS knockdown (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Figure 4B-C shows cell cycle analysis data after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: Cells in the S and G2/M phase are significantly decreased upon lncEGFL7OS knockdown.
source: Accordingly, cells in the S and G2/M phase are significantly decreased.
evidence: Figure 4B-C shows cell cycle analysis data after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: lncEGFL7OS knockdown results in G1 arrest in the si-lncEGFL7OS treated cells.
source: This indicates a G1 arrest in the si-lncEGFL7OS treated cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle analysis data showing increased G0/G1 phase cells.

claim: lncEGFL7OS silencing significantly repressed EC migration in response to VEGF treatment after wound scratch.
source: Using a scratch wound assay, we found that compared to the control, lncEGFL7OS silencing significantly repressed EC migration in response to VEGF treatment after wound scratch (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Figure 4D-E shows repression of EC migration after lncEGFL7OS silencing in a scratch wound assay.

claim: Silencing of lncEGFL7OS by siRNA#1 and #2 significantly increased EC death.
source: In the control condition,~0.4% of EC cells undergo cell death, silencing of lncEGFL7OS by siRNA#1 and #2 significantly increased EC death to ~0.55% and~0.64%, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows TUNEL assay data after lncEGFL7OS silencing.

claim: Over 2000-fold lncEGFL7OS was achieved in ECs after virus infection.
source: Over 2000-fold lncEGFL7OS was achieved in ECs after virus infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2A shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating lncEGFL7OS overexpression.

claim: LncEGFL7OS overexpression enhanced angiogenesis as shown by the significantly increased total tube length compared to the controls.
source: LncEGFL7OS overexpression enhanced angiogenesis as shown by the significantly increased total tube length compared to the controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C shows enhanced angiogenesis after lncEGFL7OS overexpression.

claim: EGFL7B and C expression was dramatically decreased upon lncEGFL7OS knockdown.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, EGFL7B and C expression was dramatically decreased upon lncEGFL7OS knockdown.
evidence: Figure 5A shows qRT-PCR data of EGFL7B and EGFL7C expression after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: The downregulation of EGFL7 at protein level by lncEGFL7OS knockdown was confirmed by Western blot analysis.
source: The downregulation of EGFL7 at protein level by lncEGFL7OS knockdown was confirmed by Western blot analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows Western blot data of EGFL7 protein after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: The expression of both miR-126 and miR-126* is downregulated by lncEGFL7OS knockdown.
source: Similarly, the expression of both miR-126 and miR-126*, a microRNA located in the intron of EGFL7 gene, is also downregulated by lncEGFL7OS knockdown (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows qRT-PCR data of miR-126 and miR-126* expression after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: miR-126 has been shown to modulate MAP kinase signaling and PI3K-AKT signaling by targeting Spred-1 and PI3KR2, respectively.
source: miR-126 has been shown to modulate MAP kinase signaling and PI3K-AKT signaling by targeting Spred-1 and PI3KR2, respectively (Fish et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008a; Kuhnert et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fish et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008a; Kuhnert et al., 2008.

claim: Phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and AKT induced by VEGF was significantly reduced in ECs transfected with si-lncEGFL7OS#1 or si-lncEGFL7OS#2 compared to the controls.
source: Consistent with the downregulation of miR-126, phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and AKT induced by VEGF was significantly reduced in ECs transfected with si-lncEGFL7OS#1 or si-lncEGFL7OS#2 compared to the controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows Western blot data of ERK1/2 and AKT phosphorylation after lncEGFL7OS knockdown.

claim: A ~ 2 fold upregulation of miR-126 was observed when lncEGFL7OS is overexpressed in ECs.
source: As expected, a ~ 2 fold upregulation of miR-126 and a ~ 3 fold increase of EGFL7B were observed when lncEGFL7OS is overexpressed in ECs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2A shows qRT-PCR data of miR-126 expression after lncEGFL7OS overexpression.

claim: A ~ 3 fold increase of EGFL7B was observed when lncEGFL7OS is overexpressed in ECs.
source: As expected, a ~ 2 fold upregulation of miR-126 and a ~ 3 fold increase of EGFL7B were observed when lncEGFL7OS is overexpressed in ECs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2B shows qRT-PCR data of EGFL7B expression after lncEGFL7OS overexpression.

claim: The combination of miR-126 and EGFL7 enhanced angiogenesis in the wild-type HUVECs.
source: The combination of miR-126 and EGFL7 enhanced angiogenesis in the wild-type HUVECs, and rescued the anti-angiogenic effect of lncEGFL7OS silencing to a great extent in an EC-Fibroblast cell co-culture model (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Figure 5D-E shows rescue of the lncEGFL7OS-knockdown angiogenic phenotype by EGFL7 protein/Adeno-miR-126.

claim: The combination of miR-126 and EGFL7 rescued the anti-angiogenic effect of lncEGFL7OS silencing to a great extent in an EC-Fibroblast cell co-culture model.
source: The combination of miR-126 and EGFL7 enhanced angiogenesis in the wild-type HUVECs, and rescued the anti-angiogenic effect of lncEGFL7OS silencing to a great extent in an EC-Fibroblast cell co-culture model (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Figure 5D-E shows rescue of the lncEGFL7OS-knockdown angiogenic phenotype by EGFL7 protein/Adeno-miR-126.

claim: MAX was predicted as one of the top lncEGFL7OS-interacting proteins by lncRNA interaction prediction program catRAPID.
source: MAX was predicted as one of the top lncEGFL7OS-interacting proteins by lncRNA interaction prediction program catRAPID (Bellucci et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics prediction using the catRAPID program.

claim: lncEGFL7OS RNA was pulled down in the nuclear lysate by a Chip-grade antibody to MAX.
source: RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) assays showed that lncEGFL7OS RNA was pulled down in the nuclear lysate by a Chip-grade antibody to MAX, and this interaction was increased by lncEGFL7OS overexpression (Figure 6B).
evidence: Figure 6B shows RIP-PCR data demonstrating MAX binding to lncEGFL7OS.

claim: The interaction between lncEGFL7OS and MAX was increased by lncEGFL7OS overexpression.
source: RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) assays showed that lncEGFL7OS RNA was pulled down in the nuclear lysate by a Chip-grade antibody to MAX, and this interaction was increased by lncEGFL7OS overexpression (Figure 6B).
evidence: Figure 6B shows RIP-PCR data demonstrating enhanced MAX binding to lncEGFL7OS after overexpression.

claim: F1 fragment in the 5' end of lncEGFL7OS is the major domain that interacts with MAX protein.
source: Similar RIP RT-PCR assays demonstrated that F1 fragment in the 5' end of lncEGFL7OS is the major domain that interacts with MAX protein (Figure 6D).
evidence: Figure 6D shows RIP-PCR data demonstrating specific binding of F1 fragment to MAX.

claim: ChIP-PCR assays confirmed the specific binding of MAX to the bidirectional lncEGFL7OS/EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer region in ECs.
source: ChIP-PCR assays confirmed the specific binding of MAX to this region in ECs (Figure 6E).
evidence: Figure 6E shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating MAX binding to the promoter/enhancer region.

claim: Overexpression of lncEGFL7OS significantly increased MAX binding to the bidirectional lncEGFL7OS/EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer region.
source: Moreover, overexpression of lncEGFL7OS significantly increased MAX binding to this region.
evidence: Figure 6E shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating enhanced MAX binding after lncEGFL7OS overexpression.

claim: MAX has been shown to dimerize with MYC and stimulate histone acetylation and gene transcription.
source: MAX has been shown to dimerize with MYC and stimulate histone acetylation and gene transcription (Vervoorts et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vervoorts et al., 2003.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation assay confirmed the interaction of MAX with p300 in ECs.
source: Our co-immunoprecipitation assay confirmed the interaction of MAX with p300, a component in the p300/CBP co-activator complex that has intrinsic histone acetyltransferase activities, in ECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1B shows co-immunoprecipitation data demonstrating MAX and p300 interaction.

claim: Acetylated H3K27 (H3K27ac) was enriched in the bidirectional lncEGFL7OS/EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer region.
source: We therefore determined whether acetylated H3K27 (H3K27ac), a marker for active enhancer, is enriched in this region, and found H3K27ac was indeed enriched in the region, and this enrichment was further increased by lncEGFL7OS overexpression (Figure 6F).
evidence: Figure 6F shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating H3K27ac enrichment at the promoter/enhancer region.

claim: The enrichment of H3K27ac in the bidirectional lncEGFL7OS/EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer region was further increased by lncEGFL7OS overexpression.
source: We therefore determined whether acetylated H3K27 (H3K27ac), a marker for active enhancer, is enriched in this region, and found H3K27ac was indeed enriched in the region, and this enrichment was further increased by lncEGFL7OS overexpression (Figure 6F).
evidence: Figure 6F shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating enhanced H3K27ac enrichment after lncEGFL7OS overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of lncEGFL7OS-F(2 + 3) neither affected EGFL7B and miR-126 expression, nor impacted angiogenesis in an EC-fibroblast co-culture assay.
source: Overexpression of lncEGFL7OS-F(2 + 3) by adenovirus neither affected EGFL7B and miR-126 expression, nor impacted angiogenesis in an EC-fibroblast co-culture assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F), suggesting the requirement of lncEGFL7OS/MAX interaction in angiogenesis.
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-F shows that lncEGFL7OS-F(2+3) overexpression does not affect EGFL7B, miR-126 expression or angiogenesis.

claim: MAX silencing resulted in significantly decreased expression of EGFL7, lncEGFL7OS and miR-126.
source: MAX silencing resulted in significantly decreased expression of EGFL7, lncEGFL7OS and miR-126 (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: Figure 6H-J shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating downregulation of EGFL7, lncEGFL7OS and miR-126 after MAX silencing.

claim: MAX silencing led to repressed angiogenesis as shown by EC-Fibroblast co-culture assays.
source: Consistently, MAX silencing led to repressed angiogenesis as shown by EC-Fibroblast co-culture assays (Figure 6K).
evidence: Figure 6K shows quantification of vessel density after MAX silencing in EC-Fibroblast co-culture assays.

claim: The induction of miR-126 expression by lncEGFL7OS overexpression was blunted by MAX knockdown.
source: As shown in Figure 6L, the induction of miR-126 expression by lncEGFL7OS overexpression was blunted by MAX knockdown.
evidence: Figure 6L shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating that MAX silencing blunts miR-126 induction by lncEGFL7OS.

claim: Silencing of lncEGFL7OS significantly reduced MAX binding to the EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer.
source: As shown in Figure 7A–B, silencing of lncEGFL7OS significantly reduced MAX binding to the EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer as well as H3K27 acetylation at the locus.
evidence: Figure 7A shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating reduced MAX binding after lncEGFL7OS silencing.

claim: Silencing of lncEGFL7OS significantly reduced H3K27 acetylation at the EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer.
source: As shown in Figure 7A–B, silencing of lncEGFL7OS significantly reduced MAX binding to the EGFL7/miR-126 promoter/enhancer as well as H3K27 acetylation at the locus.
evidence: Figure 7B shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating reduced H3K27 acetylation after lncEGFL7OS silencing.

claim: Cyclin D2 and DHFR were confirmed to be MAX targets in ECs by siRNA experiments and ChIP assays.
source: These two genes were confirmed to be MAX targets in ECs by siRNA experiments and ChIP assays (Figure 7C–D and G–H).
evidence: Figure 7C-D shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating downregulation of Cyclin D2 and DHFR after MAX knockdown, and Figure 7G-H shows ChIP-PCR data demonstrating MAX binding to their promoters.

claim: Overexpression of lncEGFL7OS enhanced the expression of Cyclin D2 and DHFR.
source: Overexpression of lncEGFL7OS enhanced the expression of Cyclin D2 and DHFR (Figure 7E–F), which could be explained by the increased binding of MAX and increased H3K27 acetylation at their respective promoters (Figure 7G–J).
evidence: Figure 7E-F shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating upregulation of Cyclin D2 and DHFR after lncEGFL7OS overexpression.

claim: Neither Cyclin D2 nor DHFR expression was repressed by lncEGFL7OS knockdown.
source: However, neither Cyclin D2 nor DHFR expression was repressed by lncEGFL7OS knockdown (Figure 7K–L).
evidence: Figure 7K-L shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating no effect of lncEGFL7OS knockdown on Cyclin D2 and DHFR expression.

claim: lncEGFL7OS does not act in trans to regulate angiogenesis through MAX under normal conditions.
source: These data suggest that, although lncEGFL7OS is capable of regulating other MAX target genes when overexpressed, lncEGF7OS does not act in trans to regulate angiogenesis through MAX under normal conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that lncEGFL7OS knockdown does not affect Cyclin D2 and DHFR expression.

claim: Lentivirus expressing sgRNA-1 or sgRNA-2 significantly repressed EC angiogenesis only when dCas9-KRAB was co-expressed.
source: By EC-fibroblast co-culture assay, lentivirus expressing sgRNA-1 or sgRNA-2 significantly repressed EC angiogenesis only when dCas9-KRAB was co-expressed (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: Figure 8B-C shows that sgRNA-mediated repression of angiogenesis requires dCas9-KRAB co-expression.

claim: Lenti-dCas9-KRAB alone did not significantly impact angiogenesis.
source: Of note, Lenti-dCas9-KRAB alone did not significantly impact angiogenesis, ruling out the potential side-effects of dCas9-KRAB overexpression.
evidence: Figure 8B-C shows that dCas9-KRAB alone does not affect angiogenesis.

claim: The expression of EGFL7B, miR-126 and lncEGFL7OS was drastically repressed by sgRNA-1.
source: When gene expression near this locus was examined, the expression of EGFL7B, miR-126 and lncEGFL7OS was drastically repressed by sgRNA-1, and to a less extent by sgRNA-2 (Figure 8D).
evidence: Figure 8D shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating downregulation of EGFL7B, miR-126 and lncEGFL7OS by sgRNA-1.

claim: The expression of EGFL7B, miR-126 and lncEGFL7OS was repressed to a less extent by sgRNA-2.
source: When gene expression near this locus was examined, the expression of EGFL7B, miR-126 and lncEGFL7OS was drastically repressed by sgRNA-1, and to a less extent by sgRNA-2 (Figure 8D).
evidence: Figure 8D shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating downregulation of EGFL7B, miR-126 and lncEGFL7OS by sgRNA-2.

claim: lncRNA-based clustering appeared to be a stronger classifier for EC lines than mRNA clustering.
source: By hierarchical cluster analysis, lncRNA-based clustering appeared to be a stronger classifier for EC lines than mRNA clustering.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: lncRNAs exhibit better tissue specificity than mRNAs.
source: This is consistent with the general perception that lncRNAs exhibit better tissue specificity than mRNAs (Derrien et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Derrien et al., 2012.

claim: Significant variability in lncRNA expression was found among EC lines.
source: We also found significant variability in lncRNA expression among EC lines, consistent the observed heterogeneity among ECs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the microarray expression data.

claim: EGFL7 encodes an EGF-like domain containing protein that is specifically secreted by vascular ECs.
source: EGFL7 encodes an EGF-like domain containing protein that is specifically secreted by vascular ECs (Parker et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parker et al., 2004.

claim: EGFL7 is conserved among vertebrates but an orthologue is also found in Drosophila melanogaster (CG7447).
source: It is conserved among vertebrates but an orthologue is also found in Drosophila melanogaster (CG7447) (Nikolic et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nikolic et al., 2010.

claim: miR-126 and miR-126* are encoded by the intron of EGFL7, and are conserved from Fugu in vertebrates to homo sapiens.
source: miR-126 and miR-126* are encoded by the intron of EGFL7, and are conserved from Fugu in vertebrates to homo sapiens (Wang et al., 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2008a.

claim: miR-126 and miR-126* are the only miRNAs that are known to be specifically in EC lineage and hematopoietic stem cells.
source: They are the only miRNAs that are known to be specifically in EC lineage and hematopoietic stem cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss-of-function studies in mice and zebrafish revealed an important function of miR-126 in governing vascular integrity and angiogenesis.
source: Loss-of-function studies in mice and zebrafish revealed an important function of miR-126 in governing vascular integrity and angiogenesis (Fish et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fish et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008a.

claim: Egfl7-/- mice display similar vascular abnormalities to MiR126-/- mice, including edema, defective cranial vessel and retinal vascularization.
source: Egfl7-/- mice display similar vascular abnormalities to MiR126-/- mice, including edema, defective cranial vessel and retinal vascularization (Schmidt et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 2007.

claim: An independent study suggests that the vascular phenotype of Egfl7-/- mice could be attributed to the MiR126 deletion (or downregulation) in the mice.
source: However, an independent study suggests that the vascular phenotype of Egfl7-/- mice could be attributed to the MiR126 deletion (or downregulation) in the mice (Kuhnert et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kuhnert et al., 2008.

claim: miR-126 has documented functions in vascular inflammation, as well as innate and adaptive immunity.
source: Besides, miR-126 also has documented functions in vascular inflammation, as well as innate and adaptive immunity (Harris et al., 2008; Mattes et al., 2009; Agudo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harris et al., 2008; Mattes et al., 2009; Agudo et al., 2014.

claim: EGFL7 is essential for vascular tube formation during vasculogenesis in zebrafish.
source: EGFL7 is essential for vascular tube formation during vasculogenesis in zebrafish (Parker et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parker et al., 2004.

claim: Targeted deletion of miR-126 in mice or miR-126 knockdown in zebrafish resulted in loss of vascular integrity and defective angiogenesis.
source: Targeted deletion of miR-126 in mice or miR-126 knockdown in zebrafish resulted in loss of vascular integrity and defective angiogenesis, while overexpression of miR-126 regulates angiogenesis in a cell-type and strand-specific manner (Fish et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008a; Kuhnert et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fish et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008a; Kuhnert et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Overexpression of miR-126 regulates angiogenesis in a cell-type and strand-specific manner.
source: Targeted deletion of miR-126 in mice or miR-126 knockdown in zebrafish resulted in loss of vascular integrity and defective angiogenesis, while overexpression of miR-126 regulates angiogenesis in a cell-type and strand-specific manner (Fish et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008a; Kuhnert et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fish et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008a; Kuhnert et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: lncEGFL7OS enhances the transcription of EGFL7/miR-126 by binding to MAX protein that is recruited to the bidirectional promoter/enhancer region in EGFL7/miR-126.
source: LncEGFL7OS enhances the transcription of EGFL7/miR-126 by binding to MAX protein that is recruited to the bidirectional promoter/enhancer region in EGFL7/miR-126.
evidence: This is based on RIP and ChIP experiments showing lncEGFL7OS/MAX interaction and MAX binding to the promoter/enhancer region.

claim: The enrichment of H3K27 acetylation by lncEGFL7OS likely result from the recruitment of CBP and P300 by MAX/MYC.
source: Based on our results showing interaction of MAX and p300, the enrichment of H3K27 acetylation by lncEGFL7OS likely result from the recruitment of CBP and P300 by MAX/MYC.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing MAX and p300 interaction, and the ChIP data showing increased H3K27 acetylation.

claim: lncEGFL7OS acts in cis by interacting with MAX transcription factor to enhance H3K7 acetylation and promote EGFL7/miR-126 expression.
source: Taken together, lncEGFL7OS acts in cis by interacting with MAX transcription factor to enhance H3K7 acetylation and promote EGFL7/miR-126 expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanistic findings from the study.

claim: Increased expression of proangiogenic factors, including hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) and VEGF-A, have been found in DCM.
source: Increased expression of proangiogenic factors, including hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) and VEGF-A, have been found in DCM, likely due to the compensatory angiogenesis and/or increased mobilization of endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) to the diseased heart (Roura et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roura et al., 2007.

claim: AMD is the leading cause of blindness in the elderly.
source: AMD is the leading cause of blindness in the elderly, and choroidal neovascularization is a hallmark for wet AMD (Jager et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jager et al., 2008.

claim: Choroidal neovascularization is a hallmark for wet AMD.
source: AMD is the leading cause of blindness in the elderly, and choroidal neovascularization is a hallmark for wet AMD (Jager et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jager et al., 2008.

claim: Anti-VEGF agents can markedly improve the clinical outcome of wet AMD.
source: Although anti-VEGF agents can markedly improve the clinical outcome of wet AMD, they have been unable to induce complete angiogenesis regression, and only 30–40% of individuals experienced vision improvement after treatment (Folk and Stone, 2010; Krüger Falk et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Folk and Stone, 2010; Krüger Falk et al., 2013.

claim: Anti-VEGF agents have been unable to induce complete angiogenesis regression in wet AMD.
source: Although anti-VEGF agents can markedly improve the clinical outcome of wet AMD, they have been unable to induce complete angiogenesis regression, and only 30–40% of individuals experienced vision improvement after treatment (Folk and Stone, 2010; Krüger Falk et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Folk and Stone, 2010; Krüger Falk et al., 2013.

claim: Only 30–40% of individuals experienced vision improvement after anti-VEGF treatment for wet AMD.
source: Although anti-VEGF agents can markedly improve the clinical outcome of wet AMD, they have been unable to induce complete angiogenesis regression, and only 30–40% of individuals experienced vision improvement after treatment (Folk and Stone, 2010; Krüger Falk et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Folk and Stone, 2010; Krüger Falk et al., 2013.
